attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, endorsed.

semantics.note: Narrowing 'it' to automating people away fits the context. But 'it doesn't work' is sweeping rhetoric with no standard for 'work', so it is better classed as rhetoric than as a checkable observation.

contract.note: The contract rightly finds no plain standard for 'working' and treats the claim as uncheckable. Any test would rest on a measure the speaker never gave.

evidence.note: Klarna's 2024 press release about itself. A company disclosure with no agreed standard to judge it against, so context only.
May 2025 report that Klarna partly reversed course. Shows the answer depends on what 'working' means. Context only.

reviews.rationale: This is a rhetorical claim that the push to automate people away does not work, with no measure of 'working'. Klarna's 2024 claims and its 2025 partial reversal point in different directions depending on the standard used. No ordinary reading settles it, so it is not adjudicable.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, endorsed.

semantics.note: The wording is close to the source. But 'barely approximated a thing society wanted or needed' is a value judgment about the worth of LLM output, not a measurable claim about demand.

contract.note: Measuring 'wanted' by user counts is the drafter's reading, and it is stretched against the speaker. In the same post he heads off that rebuttal, saying how many users ChatGPT has is not his point. The support condition also brings back the business-substitution gloss that the drafter had removed.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own statement of 500M weekly users, March 2025. A company disclosure. It speaks to usage, not to the speaker's value claim.
NBER paper with OpenAI-employed authors. Data run to July 2025, past the target period. Shows mostly personal use. Context only.

reviews.rationale: The statement judges whether LLM output met real social wants or needs. The contract turns this into a usage-count test that the speaker explicitly set aside in the same piece. That reading is not fair to his words, and there is no ordinary measure of 'society wanted or needed', so the claim is not adjudicable.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, endorsed.

semantics.note: A faithful causal summary. It leaves out the side clause about Google, which is context and not part of the core claim.

contract.note: Requiring a rise in AI content, worse information quality, and attribution follows his literal 'because of' wording. But tying the effect to two individuals requires interpretation.

evidence.note: GPTZero's report of Graphite data: AI-written articles at 36% within 12 months and 48% by 24 months. Supports only the volume part. It says nothing about quality or about Altman or Nadella.
October 2025 measurement, after the target period, finding AI articles mostly absent from search results. Context only.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows a large rise in AI-written web articles after ChatGPT. It has no measurement of information quality within the period and nothing tying the effect to OpenAI or Microsoft, let alone to Altman or Nadella. The only evidence on whether AI content reaches search users is from after the period. The causal claim is not settled.
